An augury is a sign or omen that is believed to hint at what will happen in the future.

Think of it this way: imagine you're about to start something important — a journey, a business, a battle — and right at that moment, a strange or striking thing happens around you. Maybe a flock of birds suddenly flies overhead, or a storm rolls in from nowhere, or a rainbow appears at just the right moment. In the old way of thinking — and still in a poetic, literary sense today — that event would be an augury: a message from the world (or from fate, or from the gods) about what lies ahead.

It is not just any coincidence. An augury is specifically something that is read as a prediction — a glimpse into what is coming.

The word "augury" carries two closely related meanings, and understanding both will make you confident using it in any context.

1. The sign or omen itself

This is the most common modern use. An augury is the actual thing — the event, the symbol, the natural occurrence — that seems to predict the future.

"The unexpected thunderstorm on the morning of the launch felt like an augury of disaster."

"Her warm welcome from the committee was an augury of success."

Here, the storm is the augury. The warm welcome is the augury. The sign and the augury are the same thing.

2. The practice of reading such signs

Augury also refers to the act of observing and interpreting signs to predict the future. In ancient Rome, specially appointed priests (called augurs) would watch the flight of birds — their direction, their speed, how many there were, whether they flew in formation — and interpret all of this as divine guidance about whether a particular action (going to war, holding an election, signing a treaty) would turn out well or badly. This whole ritual practice of reading natural signs was called augury.

So you might encounter sentences like:

"The general refused to march until the priests had performed their augury."

In this sense, augury is more like a ritual or discipline — the system of sign-reading itself, not just a single sign.

A crucial thing to understand: an augury is neutral by nature. It can point toward something good or something bad. This is why you will often see it paired with descriptive words:

  • "A good augury" — a sign that something positive is coming.
  • "An ill augury" / "a bad augury" — a sign that something negative is coming.
  • "An augury of doom" — a sign that disaster is ahead.
  • "An augury of hope" — a sign that better times are coming.

"The early rains, arriving just in time, were seen as a good augury for the harvest."

"The collapse of the negotiations on the very first day was an ill augury for peace."
What Makes It Different from Just Saying "Sign"?

You might wonder: why not just say "sign" or "clue"? The difference is important.

A sign is simply an indicator — neutral, factual, sometimes scientific. A road sign, a sign of fever, a sign that someone is nervous. Very everyday.

An augury, by contrast, carries a sense of fate, mystery, and prophetic weight. It suggests that the universe — or nature, or some higher force — is communicating something about the future. It has a grander, more solemn quality. It implies that the event is not just a random coincidence but a meaningful one.

This is why "augury" is used in literary, formal, or dramatic contexts — not in everyday casual speech. You would not say, "The wet umbrella by the door was an augury that it rained today." That's just a normal sign. But you would say:

"The silence that fell over the crowd the moment he walked in felt like an augury — as though even the room sensed that nothing would be the same after this."

That weight, that sense of fate being revealed, is what makes something an augury.

Today, "augury" is not a word you will hear in casual conversation. It lives in formal writing, literature, journalism, and speeches — anywhere the writer wants to add a sense of drama, weight, or prophetic significance.

Some real-world style examples:

"The early polling numbers, while not conclusive, are an augury of a difficult campaign ahead."

"The company's disastrous first quarter was an augury of the collapse that followed six months later."

"For many in the crowd, the sunrise on that historic morning felt like an augury of a new era."

Notice that in all these cases, the speaker is looking at something present and using it to suggest something about the future. That forward-pointing quality — this thing now hints at that thing to come — is always at the heart of augury.

It's worth knowing the connected verb because you will almost certainly encounter it: to augur.

  • "This augurs well." → This is a good sign for the future.
  • "This augurs badly." → This is a worrying sign.
  • "The early reviews do not augur well for the film."

The verb "augur" is actually used more frequently in modern English than the noun "augury," but they are two sides of the same coin. If something augurs well, it is a good augury.

That is the full power of augury.
